review: The Legend of Minecraft Breath of the Pokemon. Basically what this game is.

Craftopia.

This is the first time I have ever written a Review for a game.  And I will try my hardest not to drop any spoilers.

At the time of writing this, I have logged 39.8 hours in the 3 days I have owned this and don't want to stop playing.  It's been a long time since an Early Access game has caught my attention like this.  Almost to the point of Addiction. (lol).  So lets begin.

The game is an amalgamation (from my perspective) of game features, that, just seem to work well together.  At first when I started playing, it reminded me of Genshin Impact.  The third person View, the ease of controls.  The more I played, the more I found.  

Features

Crafting – I don't think I need to explain this feature.  But the crafting system is (even though its still in early development) quite extensive.  You gain more crafting stations as you progress your “AGE” (more on that to come)  

Taming – This reminds me of (and please don't laugh), Pokemon.  You craft “Monster Prisms”, then bring a Monster to near death, then “throw” said Prism, to catch the Monster.  You can then either breed  them, use them, and I believe, even have them fight with you. (I've seen a skill that makes your pet attack)

Building – Build your house.  Seems basic, But as you progress your “Age” you get more and better options for building your Dream house.

Exploration – Exploration is accomplished with the “Door of Transportation”. {insert accual name} New Islands are opened up through spending Resources.  Higher level Islands Require more and higher resources.

Skill Tree – There are 5 Skill Trees.  Skill points are acquired through leveling and completing Sub-missions (Main Mission is not implemented as of yet)
Basic – these are your Basic Skills.  Stamina, jumping, ect...
Combat – What kind of Character do you wanna play?  The Archer, The Warrior, The Mage, Maybe a Monk or a Knight.  Play how you like.
Magic – This is where your Spells live.  If anything,  Get Heal and Resurrection. (just my opinion to)
Living – Passives to increase your gathering skills.
Trick – Best description I can come up with is Miscellaneous Skills.

There is a Second section in the skills that is not implemented as of yet.

Multiplayer
Yes, there is a Multiplayer system in place, albeit, buggy at the moment.

Automation System
You can Automate almost every gathering aspect of this game from what I've seen so far.

Quest System
At this moment in the Games development, there is no Main Mission/Quest line, But there are sub-missions to wet your appetite.

There's bound to be more that I haven't found yet, or have forgotten.  Plus, the devs will most likely add more.

Pros
-The skill system is really nice.  Lets you customize how you want to play your character.  
-The Gathering and Crafting system is Good to.  Lots to build and enjoy.
-Automation.  I'm really just starting to play with this, but, I like the fact that I can go explore another Island, and production will continue.

Cons
-Multiplayer.  I do understand that Craftopia is still in Early Access. That being said, At times it works great, other times its a nightmare.  My biggest thing with it is that, when you travel to another island, every one who is playing in the current world will be transported with you.  My wife likes to build, and I like to gather and explore.

Overall Impressions 
I, Personally, am looking forward to see what the Devs have planned for the future of this game.  Even though Multiplayer is a big issue at the moment, I have faith the Devs will fix this soon.  Single player and Multiplayer play exactly the same (atm), so you can play Single Player, learn the system, and then when Multiplayer is flushed out, you already know what to do.  And for $25, I think its well worth the price.

Great game, especially for playing with friends. I'm sure that ya'll have seen the other reviews talking about how 'waah, they removed 90% of the content' and so on in regards to the new Seamless World update. Allow me to explain a bit, so you can see why this isn't actually a problem. Originally, the game had one island you would start on, with a limited world-space. However, you could build portals to traverse to new island worlds. It worked a little like how Minecraft handles going to the nether, except it was other islands. Each was their own biome, with a decent bit of variation in enemies and resources.

What this Seamless World update did was get rid of that world style. Instead, they changed it so that, instead of a bunch of small worlds that you used portals to go between, you instead have one large landmass that you can explore and adventure on much like Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild or Genshin Impact has. They did leave out a large chunk of features from the game when they made the switch however, and this is what people are getting hung up on.

Simply put, the content is not GONE, but rather rearranged. Some things are in the game and people just don't realize that they are because they have yet to encounter them, either due to rarity, placement, or other things. As for the rest, they wanted to get this update out so we could play and enjoy it as soon as they could. This meant that, even though not all of the content from those island biomes had been placed in the world, we're getting it much sooner. In other words, the some 30% of things that aren't in the game currently are only not in the game for a temporary length of time while they work on fitting them into the new design, since disjointed island biomes are very different from the far more continuous and connected design of the new world. Just give it some time, and it'll all be back.

~~~~~~

In conclusion, it's a very fun game, and definitely worth picking up. The asking price of ~$25 is honestly a steal in my opinion, and, if you can get it on sale, even better. It has fun mechanics and, even though it isn't super well written, a rather funny story. The combat generally feels pretty fluid, striking somewhere between a soulslike and the aforementioned Breath of the Wild. It has adjustable difficulties, letting it be as casual or as hard as you want with a custom one. Modding, courtesy of BepInEx's modloader and the Steam workshop. Lots of RPG elements, such as levels, varied equipments, potions, skill trees, etc. And you can even use the monster taming system to basically play Pokémon instead of the normal fighting, if that's more your speed.

Frankly, this game has just about everything, and is definitely a hidden gem. Could not recommend more. :)

Alright I played enough of this game that I think I can give a fair review.

The Good: 

Fun gameplay, solid graphics, combat feels good (melee, magic, and bows atm), the crafting/gathering is solid, the talent system is good.

The OK:

Base building can be annoying, placement of objects seems to bug out sometimes, there are exploit regarding planting crops that can give you tons of crops without much space, some of the automated mechanics (machines and robots) are wonky and while they work they get stuck sometimes. Animal breeding for foods/feces/batteries is very annoying to manage. 

Items have different affixes that change the enchants of whatever they are used to craft. (i.e wolf/sheep/cow/elephant leather have different enchants and when crafted into armor provide those enchants). This means that none of the items stack with the same items from other animals.

The dungeon is the same everytime (minus the race/ball/jump challenges) with only a different boss sometimes.

The Bad:

Inventory - Chests provide absolutely criminal low storage when items don't stack with each other. You will literally need like 3 of the largest chest just to hold 1 type of item (all the different leathers for example). Character inventory is criminal as well considering the above. You will need to frequently do inventory management.

Weapon Durability - You literally just spend money when you repair your items and its not even a lot of money, and they break so fast. It's just an extra chore in a game with plenty of chores.

Enchanting Gear - This one broke me. This is the only reason I cannot recommend this game and it is why I stopped playing it. RNG on RNG. As I mentioned, crafting materials have affixes on them to enchant your gear so here is how it works.

Say you want to make a SPECIFIC enchanted hat with 4 (the max) enchants on it and it takes 1 steel (which is 5 iron) and 1 wood. Let's say the affixes you are looking for are "Wolf" "Cow" "Sheep" "Fire Spirit". You will need to acquire 1 Fire Spirit log from the volcano biome. Easy enough. Now for the Wolf Cow Sheep Steel Bar. You acquire some Iron with each affix. Now you smelt them and HOPE you get "Wolf Cow Sheep Steel Bar" but it can be 0-all affixes on the bar. you gotta hope you craft a bar that nabs all 3. This will take a lot of bars or a lot of luck.

You get lucky, you have your Fire Spirit log and your Wolf Cow Sheep Steel Bar so you craft your hat, but the same rules apply. Now you need to hope your hat rolls all 4 affixes but it can roll any combination of 1, 2, 3, or 4 of the affixes. You don't get the hate you need, go back to step one. Some items have you repeat this process more than twice.

I spent 4 hours acquiring materials to make a new shield and the end result was enough Steel to make 1 attempt at the shield, I did not get it.


TLDR - RNG killed this game for me, otherwise its a really solid game.

So, recently i have been going trough my Early Access purchases to weed out the chaff that clearly has gone awry. And as you can see Craftopia has hit that criterium, for now at least.
Here are Craftopia's most pressing problems:

There is a lot of stuff in this game. Really a lot. However, everything is... just unfinished and disconnected.

This game has building with prefab parts, like different walls, slopes, roof tiles, instead minute blocks. Like for example Valheim, which is fine and works well in other games. However, building and placing these parts is inaccurate at best and a broken at worst. It just feels wrong and anything build is just janky.

There is crafting, but it is not really finished in any way. Within literally 1 hour you can go from nothing to silver (basically tier 4) weapons and tools. There is also no real flow to drive you to make better stuff because what you use tools on and for is just no fun.
There are the roots of automation, but the whole thing is very illogical, contrived and janky. It is also not worth doing because there is not really anything you are doing this FOR (we come back to this part later again).

There are dungeons, but they are plain garbage. Built from the same few assets, flatly lit, ugly and without any atmosphere or flair. And they have nothing going for them that could remotely be called level design.

There are vehicles, but the controls are utter garbage. I found a race dungeon with hover boards and speed up pads but it was so bad i'd rather tried to finish it on foot.

There is combat, but it is stiff, flailing and floaty.

There are rarity and status prefixes for loot and items (like flaming, freezing etc.). But those can be attached to ANY item, weapon or consumable! Which leads to your inventory often filling with the same type of item that need 5 different fields in your inventory because they have different prefixes. 

This one needs a bit more explaining. Imagine, if you will, you kill a few cows. The cows then drop horns and leather and so on. Every piece of leather and every horn could theoretically have a different prefix, like fiery cows horn and scary cows horn, stuff like that. And any time this is a case these items need their own field in your inventory. Now there is a lot of space in your inventory to begin with. But the issue is that this makes no sense whatsoever, it serves no purpose and just causes a mess that adds NOTHING to the gameplay. 

That also counts for the prefixes on weapons. Because the differences between them feel minuscule and I am not putting in the time it would need to fill out that massive skill tree so it MAYBE makes a difference way later. 

A Story isn't there. Just forget it.
Translation is classic engrish.

Even the most basic things in this game work in janky ways. Raising the FOV for example, doesn't actually raise the FOV, it zooms out the camera. Setting the FOV to 100 moves the camera so far from your character that it is hard to play. 
Trying to open and use items (and I mentioned building earlier) is janky as hell and collision detection is a mess. Trying to open a chest that has been placed between crafting tables or other chests is a mess causing the player to regularly open or activate something that is nowhere near your Crosshair.

Crafting tables, workstations and building elements have INDIVIDUAL PHYSICS. Meaning they could be kicked around and have collision detection and physics. Anyone that remembers early 2000s physics knows what happens next. Sometimes when you load into your world, tables or building elements have fallen trough the world or other building parts. Or you have to search your entire base for the one tiny thing that causes a constant collision sound because it slipped into a another object somehow, somewhere. 

There are more issues with this unfocused disaster. However, the worst part is that NONE of it feels like it serves a uniting vision. There is no reason for the crafting and the automation and the vehicles and EVERYTHING else!
At no point does it feel the the developers have a encompassing vision for these disparate parts nor does it feel like they have the ability and focus to give any of them the necessary base finish or polish.

This game ultimately feels cheap and shallow to play. It feels like a waste of time, especially when Steam is full off better alternatives. Don't waste your time. Maybe come back far later. 

Though considering that the team clearly has bitten off too much AND are starting development on a second game that looks eerily similar in many aspects, I would not count on it.

Of course, if this improves one day, and i'll notice it, then I will update this review.

I'm a game developer. Last year, I spent 40 minutes in a call explaining how this game had accidentally solved one of the biggest problems in open world level design: The feeling that there's plenty to explore, but not much incentive to do so. The enchanting system, at that time, was accidentally genius. Why "accidentally?" Because these guys can't make anything that isn't buggier than a $200 New York apartment. And yet they'd implemented a series of integrated systems that would set the player out on a journey across 10 biomes to do something as mundane as harvesting wood... I'd be fighting dragons in Hell just to get a bundle of logs with a "More Scorching" enchantment. There wasn't just a big world, but there was this integral reason to want to go everywhere, even if your goal for today was small and specific like "craft a new shield upgrade."

Then they dropped this Seamless World Update.

Ignoring that the bugs are far worse than I remember, across every field (animation hangs, armor clipping, AI just outright breaking or running an infinite loop (even teleporting back to the start and repeating after each loop) etc.. But no, they took the one thing they'd done exceptionally and made it the most mundane, "20 minute a day" mobile grind you could imagine:

Know how you get enchantments now? Open Map. Teleport to dungeon door. Fight easy boss. Get a pile of 1 time use scrolls, containing random enchantments. Repeat. Mindlessly. For eternity. Just spam the exact same fight, over and over and over..

And while you're at it: be aware that the seamless world update REMOVED bosses (approximately half of all existing bosses if not more), REMOVED 2 out of 7 ages (the end-game progression arcs) and REMOVED MOST (At least 70, probably more likely 90%) of enemy types. Content from two years ago is no longer present.

So basically, they watered down the best mechanic they had, removed the best part of the game, removed a good portion of bosses, bugged it all to hell and back (sadly Hell no longer exists) and lost all of their unique individuality that made this game stand out despite being programmed in such a buggy, poorly optimized, amateur way, all to make it a more "digestible" variant of so many nearly identically pointless games where you just loop the exact same behavior over and over with no real reason or incentive to do so.

As a programmer, artist, animator, and everything else.. I am entirely self taught. So it's pretty bad that I can so openly criticize the implementation this badly. Because with all of 3 years of experience, I don't have a single prototype that's as badly programmed as this whole game.

I enjoyed it despite that. Then returned to see what the Seamless World update would add. I'm sorry, but I see nothing worth recommending since that update. Everything good was removed and replaced with the most watered down, restricted, repetitive version you could possibly imagine.

Oh, and they removed most of the build system's snap and placement logic, too. You can't change the voxel size for building placement anymore. Just one poorly planned giant grid and nothing else.

[strike]45 hours in, I still haven't gotten bored.[/strike] [i]80-something hours in, I still haven't gotten bored.[/i]

This game [u]WAS[/u] a buggy mess, multiplayer [u]USED TO BE[/u] fucked and the gameplay loop can still feel kinda same-y and repetitive. This game is like if you let a child open five different flavors of ice cream out of the freezer, throw some of each in a bowl, and stirred it around until it all turned into a weird, brown soup with little "unique" bits sticking out of it everywhere. That said, that's a sweet fucking soup and dear god does this game not lack in the charm-department.

This game still draws HEAVILY on some BOTW themes, through the lenses of the same toddler who didn't think the anime Arifureta was a comedy. Thematically, and with quite a few of the basic gameplay elements, you'll find it wears Zelda not just on it's sleeve, but printed all over it's grimy t-shirt and sweatpants. Underneath that hyper-stylized (and honestly, still gorgeous) art/world design, you'll find some really quite sophisticated guts holding it up. This game will scratch your itch for everything from Factorio to Diablo, and it'll still have you playing five different slot machines at the end of the day.

You can pretty much draw connections between any games you want, but if the above sounds interesting, go for it. 25 bucks is still less than you wasted on [insert more relevant game that flopped on release than Cyberpunk here].

[i]I'd also like to say, holy shit, the skills and build options are only getting better and better as time goes on. No other game will let you not only enslave children inside pokeballs, but also build your character around releasing said children only to cause them to explode in order to kill your enemies.[/i]

I don't normally write reviews, but I felt compelled to for this one because I've played both before and after the Seamless World update.

     A lot of people are criticizing the developers for switching to a seamless world, claiming it removed 70% of the game's content. From my experience, that simply isn't true. The content hasn't been removed—much of it is currently locked behind the Age progression system. I've personally verified this using the Sivet Command Workshop Mod, which shows that many of the items people claim were removed still exist in the game. They're just not immediately accessible.

     The same applies to certain world bosses and dungeon bosses, although I won't go into detail there. What I will point out is that this is an Early Access game. Steam's own Early Access guidelines make it clear that a game can be significantly different by the time it reaches full release.

     I've also noticed that many of the negative reviews come from players with fewer than 200 hours played, while a lot of the more detailed positive reviews come from players with 250+ hours. That's not to say hours played automatically make an opinion more valid, but it does provide additional context.

     That said, I'm not completely thrilled about some previously available items being locked behind Ages again. However, very few people seem willing to discuss the issues that existed before Seamless World. On the Legacy branch, I could open 15 Cherry Blossom biomes and still not get any Residential tiles. I even had an entire map layer that was practically unusable. I remember having to completely reset one area of my map over 20 times just to find a biome I had never encountered before. Those problems existed long before Seamless World, yet they rarely get mentioned.

     Another thing worth noting is timing. Most of the negative reviews appeared within the first week after the update launched. I'm writing this review roughly a month later, after having more time to actually experience the changes. This review is largely a response to the criticism that seems to overlook some important facts.

     If you don't enjoy the current Seamless World version, the developers have given players alternatives. You can go into the game's settings, select the Betas tab, and switch to the Legacy branch. If you want access to content like Brigandine Valley before the planned updates, you can even use the Alpha branch, understanding that it comes with additional bugs and instability. The developers have provided options, which is more than many Early Access games do.

     I'm not a game developer or a professional critic. I'm just a player. I understand that both positive and negative reviews reflect individual experiences, and everyone is entitled to their own opinion. All I ask is that people don't treat any single review—positive or negative—as absolute truth.

     Instead, look at gameplay footage yourself. Watch videos from both the Legacy version and the Seamless World version. Compare them, look at the current state of the game, and make your own decision based on the evidence rather than relying entirely on someone else's opinion.

Looking at this game now, it's a fine mess. The devs have also started a new project called Palworld, and looking at the reviews of their earlier game Overdungeon, they don't have a good track record at keeping projects alive until completion. I would skip this until much more progress is made and they show more commitment.

edit: Nothing has changed since I made this review. Please, DO NOT BUY THIS GAME.

What a pleasure this game is.

It feels like Breath of the Wild had a child with No Man's Sky and tried to teach that child the importance of The Elder Scrolls Morrowind.

As a base, the game takes a little too much from BotW, But at the end of the day, it feels like it was supposed to be mechanically anyway. Get gear, level up, craft equipment, fish, climb, cook, sell... It just feels natural. Combat is exactly what you would expect, except the part where being Link felt grounded, when the going gets rough, you can bolt away from most things and glide away, as it has two speeds. 
-It also mixes mechanics so well that if you like one concept or another, you can play on those strengths until you get the skills or gear you need to either feel comfortable with the combat, or feel comfortable with the crafting and equipment mechanics. 
-Overall, it feels like they targeted a lot of the quips people have had with crafting games such as, bad combat, areas being too large, carrying weight being too cumbersome, moving inventory to stores taking too long, etc. It isn't small, but it also isn't too big, but if you want more there are so many areas you can visit, and if you want less all you have to do is make money and get enough materials to press into new areas... Just watch your stats, you might get mowed down if you go too far.

Now, allow me to explain why the similarities are what they are in my opinion.
-The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild
Obvious... But running, exploring, combat, gliding, dungeons, loot, inventory UI, even some of the things they are going to add feel like someone loved BotW so much that they wanted to pull everything they could get away with while adding their own personal touches, even some things like skulls the goblins hide in and the excessive amounts of scout towers they look out from feels verbatim to say it lightly, heck, even the way Link gained hearts or stamina by visiting shrines is in here. But when you like something so much, but just want to add your personal touch to it, I would imagine a fan wanting to go about it the same way. Frankly, the games mechanics work so well with the feel of BotW that you might want to forgive them for borrowing a little too liberally at times, though I hope they find better ways to do so, because it feels a little overdone sometimes.

-No Man's Sky
The game spreads itself around locales that has varying levels as you progress, and as you progress, you can take any and all materials you pull from the environment aside from the door you use to leave the locale you're in and the one you arrive on. There are differing environments, habitats, enemies and resources that you can harvest, and even capture monsters and NPCs that you can bring with you across locales to build the perfect instance of whatever ecosystem you would like to have. This addition to the gameplay design allows a lot of forgiveness for the otherwise small building area, but also leaves so much untouched potential for things like survival, and randomly generated islands to take on with your friends, or alone. You could even try to be timed on how long it takes you to get to the god's alter from scratch, and get on a leaderboard or whatever. Regardless, this mechanic is basically the band aid that makes the game stronger than it should ever be if used properly.

-The Elder Scrolls: Morrowind
Now... Morrowind fans might get a little bit irritated at why this is here, but with the addition of traited equipment as well as equipment that grants a spell on it that you can cast when equipped, the game has the potential to be so intricate that it can be utterly broken in the best of ways. 
For example, equipment has a chance to adopt traits from materials to used to craft it. Normally that means using various materials and hoping that those traits get adopted, to the point where a few tries of rare equipment could expend the materials altogether. But if you make a bucket, or a ring, or an arrow... You could get those same powerful effects without having to lose your mind over the chance normally required to get those things to happen. So now your equipment bag is full of arrows, buckets and rings that allow you to adjust your character without having to flip your blacksmith desk. Far out right?! I hope they never change this. 

-Another fantastic thing about this game is the automation potential, you can breed animals you catch, mass produce crops and have robotics manage your areas with some know how. Even have mechanizations deal with ore deposits (bedrocks) that are otherwise futile to mine physically. If you have the need to do more things, there are options there that provide you the tools to automate everything you need if you get the materials to make it all. 
-There is also no weight system, so if you set out with the goal of getting ore, each item type can hold four stacks of items of its own type, and supports different inherited values too. So if you got tired of how long it took for you to move your ore and wood in other games... Just come here and play this one. You can carry like 5000 logs. I hope they up the amount of equipment space you have though, and add support for dying clothes. As it is now there are only 8 armor sets. 4 for each gender, and 4 of which are just recolors of the different two types for each gender. There are supposed to be vanity clothing coming... I'm very excited for that too.

Well, there are a few gripes that I do have, but they might not be that serious. 
-In crafting games, investment is almost necessary, maybe actually necessary. So when you buy a spell for the first time and use it, and consider starting over because you know if you put those two points into jumping you would jump twice as high, it gets pretty annoying. Do yourself a favor and try skills with a throwaway character so you don't get burned by a bad description, or a bad skill overall. They said they were using a translation thing to translate, so, it is what it is.
-Sometimes fighting an enemy over the course of a long time might make them disappear between night or day. I remember fighting a dragon and not being particularly ready offensively, and ended up watching it go up in smoke when the day was over... It might be a mechanic so you don't catch enemies you aren't technically ready for, but it freaking sucks when you go back to your base and have to sell off all the weapons you just wore down trying to fight that thing... Maybe it was a bug, but Christ if there are more challenging fights later on, I really don't want to be mechanically told that I either have to only fight things I can plow through or not even try. I beat it after I did the Morrowind thing above. But I won't expect that to be possible with future enemies.

Should you get it? I'm not sure... For me, I told myself that I wanted something like Genshin Impact to waste away on, but I lost all interest in it after I saw it was free-to-play. I played a few other crafting games like Dark and Light, and Citadel Forged in Fire, and while some of those have more intricate item gathering mechanics, and bigger maps as well as a more tolerable fast traversal option. (the hover boards are super clunky in here...imo, didn't make the others yet) Overall, this one feels the most like a game that you happen to be able to build in, instead of a game you build in, that happens to have exploration. Though I will say that other survival games handle traveling in the dark a little better. But if I'm honest, unless Monster Hunter, Lost Planet or Dragon's Dogma make a survival game with all of their mechanics intact, it'll be hard to top the limitless potential this game has. If you're like me, sure, give it a go. But if the games that come together to make a game like this satisfy you on their own? Come back when regular people are playing the game on YouTube, and draw your conclusions from there.

I have put a serious amount of time into Craftopia — through boss fights, tower repairs, age progression, farming empires, dungeon crawling, enchanting builds, and even vehicle chaos — and I can confidently say this game is far deeper than most people realize.

First, let’s address the noise.

You’ll see reviews claiming the game is “abandoned” or “never going to be finished.” Ignore them.

The developers are constantly patching, fixing bugs, and releasing updates. The update history speaks for itself. Are there bugs? Yes. Absolutely. But they are actively being worked on, and content continues to expand.

Now let’s talk about what actually matters: the systems.

Craftopia is deceptively deep.

You have:

• Multiple Age Progression systems that unlock entire tiers of technology
• Tower restoration that changes how you explore the world
• Boss Rush dungeons and open-world bosses
• Resource automation and farming systems
• Vehicle crafting (yes, including a cow-shaped motorcycle)
• Base building with scaling automation

But that’s just surface level.

The Picture Book system alone adds insane long-term depth. Craft a certain number of items and your stats permanently increase. That means everything you make contributes to progression. It rewards crafting diversity and long-term play in a way most games don’t even attempt.

Then there’s gear progression.

• Tool refining
• Weapon refinement
• Armor upgrading
• Deep enchant extraction and transfer systems
• Rare boss drops
• Build optimization

You can reskill and specialize however you want.

Want to play one-handed swords?
Heavy two-handed weapons?
Full bow/ranged build?
Guns?
Magic staff user?

The skill tree supports it. And respeccing allows experimentation.

Combat feels responsive and rewarding. Boss fights range from manageable to brutal, especially in the later biomes. And capturing bosses adds another layer entirely.

Replayability is huge.

You can:
• Focus on farming and automation
• Speedrun Age progression
• Create optimized combat builds
• Grind Picture Book stats
• Boss hunt
• Dungeon clear
• Play solo or co-op

Every time I return after a break, I find something new to optimize or improve.

Is it perfect? No.
Is it shallow? Absolutely not.

Craftopia is ambitious, layered, chaotic in the best sandbox way, and constantly improving.

If you enjoy deep progression systems, build experimentation, and games that reward long-term investment, Craftopia is absolutely worth your time.

Fantastic game. Got this a while ago and at first the multiplayer barely worked, but with subsequent patches (the devs are working hard on it) this improved and became playable.

Game has a lot of depth to it and found time after time there was an additional layer of complexity after ascending ages, or figuring out new mechanics with gear, or skill trees. The game gets even better with friends as you can actually make a composition of tank, heal (kinda) and dps, and I definitely reccommend this game to be played with friends.

The sweet spot seems to be 4 people, especially if you pick different roles, more than that and gear fighting becomes a thing as it is incredibly material consuming and RNG to get 1 set, let alone 4. Going over 4-6 people becomes a bit of a mess, especially when magic gets involved. One ice spell is particularly frustrating as it interacts with players and creates a very large impassable obstruction which can interrupt healing, abilities or trap you. As a tank I found this to be very disrupting in fights (looking at you chris).

The combat itself, while relatively deep for melee with a lot of different routes to take whether you want to go in hard with damage or tankyness, a lot of builds are viable, though there is an annoyance with archery where you are effectively "losing" a gear slot (arrows) due to firing them. 

The netcode is the game's main weakness, and this ties in heavily to combat. While I would say combat is "fun" it can be pretty frustrating with hit detection, animation lock, and ESPECIALLY in multiplayer having everyone seeing consistent results in the same combat. Often when doing a boss with a lot of abilities, different people will see abilities used on different people, or at different times, but only one or the other will be "real." The game's netcode seems to be a bit of a mess, though it's understandable for a beta game.

I have come across a few serious bugs and issues though (mostly to do with netcode) and the main one that comes to mind is where I made the mistake of building on land at ground level on the starter island. Me and a bunch of friends built a very nice and large base which Alexa very nicely decorated and arranged with chests, but due to one stray blue blob creature getting stuck undernearth, the game decided it had enough. A load of lag and audible hit detection later, I came back to the base to see that a hole had been blown from the base, all the way through multiple floors, taking out our entire chest room with it, from one small mob which got bugged in the wall, destroying half of the base. Suffice to say I've built high in the air or over water ever since.

When you get to the "endgame" you start to really notice some of the game's other flaws. While at first, dungeon variation seems pretty nice with multiple dungeon types and different end bosses on each map, by the time you've run a few they will quickly get stale and repetitive, and you have to run quite a few of these for materials, gear and stat upgrade tokens. The maps have a similar issue, where you feel like the game has endless variation until about 10 or so hours in, when you realize there's about 10 different map types repeated, leading to knowing the map's layout as soon as you arrive. However, I fully expect both of these issues to resolve the more development goes into the game, as the core building blocks, with the gearing and levelling loop being fantastic.

The game additionally has a lot of "minecraft-like" QOL stuff. You can set up self-sustaining farms, breeding plots, and automate entire mining, refining, and crafting lines if you spend a bit of time setting it up. There's also a ton of customization, both building wise and player wise, with a lot of hard-to-get cosmetics which look great and are satisfying once earned.

All in all, the game is very rough around the edges and needs a lot of development, but with friends this game is really a 9/10 and a great laugh. Just don't let Maddie near any open flames or she will set everyone and the whole base on fire.

Also dragons are cool as hecc. If you can look past the growing pains of this game, and understand it will get much better with time, then this is an easy buy.

EDIT: Forgot to mention, due to the repetitive nature of endgame, the game can get pretty boring once you're maxed out at endgame (which I was for a while) in gear, levels and achievements. Though with the newly released "hell" region, a nice degree of challenge has been added with a lot more complexity for gear, which is a nice addition. We had a blast hunting for the new age upgrade materials and battling stronger dragons while getting swarmed by waves of respawning mobs, though as usual the buggy nature of the game showed with dead bodies seemingly being able to hold aggro for a while as long as you don't hit respawn. Hopefully this is patched in the next update.
The game is very friendly to new players too, as if you know what you're doing, you can level and gear up pretty quick, catching up in no time, so you can always add new friends to the group (max size 8 online at any one time). The game is also alt-friendly and I highly reccommend have a combat character at max level, and a crafting/lifeskill character at max level. You can respec for a small cost, but it can get tedious constantly changing skills.

To directly address some of the issues I've read from negative comments:
-I've seen comments about people having issues with game saves not functioning correctly. I've had no problems with that. The game actually has a built in save backup system for restoring saves if something goes awry.
-I've seen comments about bad performance, both graphically, and with multiplayer. My GF and I play together via LAN and neither have had issues with regular performance graphics wise. We have had one session where she ran into issues. It was like on minecraft when you look at a bad chunk and your framerate tanks but but after she restarted the game everything went back to normal. (we have only ever played on LAN, we have not played on hosted servers)
-I've seen comments about the game being abandoned. They literally just posted an update 2 days ago. 
-Before buying the game I tried to find recent video reviews. The most recent I could find being from ~4 months ago. One of the main issues that was mentioned in some of those videos were a lack of fast travel. That is no longer a thing. There are waypoints you can fast travel to EVERYWHERE. 

A couple of small issues I have had are:
- The stamina bar seems to be either inconsistent in what triggers it to drain or there are some hunger mechanics at play that are not explicitly explained. At times I can take off running and the bar doesn't drain at all. Others I take off and it will start draining as expected. My glide skill is maxed yet there are occasions where my stamina drops very quickly when I start to glide. However, if I'm cliffside and make a point to let my stamina fill completely before triple jumping and gliding as far as I can I have no issues.
- As mentioned previously, there are plenty of fast travel locations. When we are playing together I host and tend to fast travel a lot. When I do and have the loading screen on my end, my GF's side does hitch and slow for moment before I'm loaded back into the new area but then performance goes back to normal for her. 
- We play primarily with controller and there are times that controls are... clunky. I have yet to figure out how to extract enchantments without grabbing the mouse but to be fair the game page does only show partial controller support.
- You will see new enemies in each area as you progress through the ages but goblins are a mainstay so get ready to kill lots of them, regular goblins, fire goblins, electric goblins, poison goblins, etc. Goblins goblins goblins. 

Overall, I've definitely got my money's worth and I'm still nowhere near done. I had this on my wishlist for a long time before I finally got it and wish I would have purchased sooner.

The endgame boils down to one thing: crafting good gear. This will make or break your experience. The crafting in this game is an elusive mechanic, and I will attempt to describe it to you so that you can better understand it before going in.

[h1] Now, one might ask, "What is possibly wrong with an incentive to craft in a game called Craftopia?" [/h1] 
The problem(s): A completely RNG driven crafting system. The difference between a base item and one with good enchantments is so astronomical that you should almost never consider using a base item over one with enchantments (exception would be a weapon with high base attack or magic attack). 

[b] Enchantments work like this: [/b] Enchantments are tied to proper words. These proper words each reflect a set of stats and can be incorporated into items through crafting materials. For instance, if an iron ingot has the proper word "Crimson" and is used to craft a sword, then the sword has a chance to receive the proper name, "Crimson" and the stats associated with the name. 

As far as I have seen, an item can hold up to four enchantments. For example an item is called "The Never Ending Sky's Ancient Veteran Griffin's Broadsword", and it has the four enchantments: "The Never Ending Sky's", "Ancient", "Veteran", and "Griffin's". Without the enchantments, a broadsword would just be that, a broadsword. On paper this system sounds really fun and interesting, but in practice the crafting is tedious and can feel completely unrewarding because of two things: no indication of success chance (or tutorial explaining the chances involved with enchanting items), and inventory management.       

[h1] Now, one might ask, "How is crafting RNG if the inputs always guarantee the outputs?" [/h1] 
The problem(s): The inputs only guarantee the base item being produced. Enchantments are, as far as I can tell, completely randomly assigned each time an item is crafted. The possible name of the item produced is pulled from the crafting materials used to produce it. I'll repeat: having crafting materials with proper names does not guarantee that crafted items will have those proper names. It is entirely possible to use a significant amount of very rare crafting materials to produce a white/common/base item! 

This is a HUGE problem when some items require dozens of crafting materials to produce just one unit. The rudimentary experience I've had with the crafting is something around 1 in 75 to 1 in 50 (~1.33% to ~2% chance) to produce an item with 4 proper names. 

Enchantments or modifiers distinguish items and crafting materials from each other. Unless an item has the same enchantments and base item, then it will not stack with items with similar bases. This leads into problems with inventory (and storage) management. Frankly, I think this problem mostly stems from the lack of inventory slots (not carry capacity), and I think it can only be resolved by introducing something like a backpack or a straight upgrade to storage/item slots. 


[h1] I will not leave the developers out on a limb here. Here is how you improve your game: [/h1]
Display roll chances for enchantments when crafting; also, improve the chances to craft said loot. People do not have the time (or patience) to slog through hours of gameplay only to come up with a white/common/base item. That leaves a really sour taste in your player's mouths and you want them to feel good about crafting gear with the loot they EARNED. 

Increase player inventory and storage SLOT amounts (not carry capacity per slot) to alleviate the item bloat that inevitably happens in the endgame. 


If none of this has dissuaded you from jumping into early access, then you'll like the game. I had fun with it myself, but I cannot earnestly recommend it to everyone in its current state.

This is a great game as long as you're aware it's not actually a factory building game like Factorio. Yes, there are mechanics that allow for partial automation, but issues will arise when using them such as farming robots disappearing/falling through floors or item drops despawning when you have too many on the ground or conveyer belts. While this will likely be fixed in future updates (such as by stacking item drops when they're near other item drops), this review is based on the game as-is.

Building: While rotating and re-orienting building placements can be somewhat annoying to figure out, you have several construction materials and can create some good-looking spaces. The game handles indoor spaces rather well, so individual rooms can be as small or large as desired. Particles will sometimes travel through buildings and birds like to fly into them.

Enchantments: The most important part of the game in my opinion. When crafting any items, you'll use potentially enchanted items. By using preferable enchanted items, you can greatly boost your stats (such as attack speed, movement speed, maximum health, etc.). This makes armor, weapon, and tool crafting much more engaging as the very resources you use will have a major (ideally beneficial) effect on the resulting product. This is even relevant to farming as the enchantments of the farm plot will carry over to the resulting crops.

Combat: The combat plays similarly to BOTW with spells and skills but with a bit less polish. Durability is a mechanic which I personally find annoying, and you'll need to grind for a while (Tip: Go to high level islands, find a few weapons, and use them in islands where your player level is recommended. Going to very high level islands does not appear to grant bonus XP and the enemies will turn into tanks that absolutely chew through your durability). Don't worry about guns as more complex weapons can be very difficult to get. Bows are surprisingly effective, especially when paired with status effects. To avoid eating excess food, take the heal skill when possible as it's very cheap for what you get.

Quests: You'll find several quest items and nobody to turn them over to because the NPCs don't ever seem to ask for them even though they're generic. You'll find the same guy over an over that sarcastically remarks, "You're giving me log?". This is the only quest I believe I've ever fulfilled.

Storage: You're going to find a very large variety of items, so you'll want to make several chests to store them. I highly recommend placing these chests on crafted floors (preferably non-flammable) so that there is no chance of them disappearing or otherwise becoming inaccessible. Items with different enchantments can use the same storage slot as long as there are no more than four different enchantment types. Most items stack to 100. Your inventory never seems to be large enough, so make sure to bring nothing with you when exploring a new island.

Automation: Some things can be only partially automated or can't be automated. Automation can be slow to set up and tedious to ensure it is working properly. For the most part automation can be bypassed, but I've found the production of wheat should be automated as flour is important in the process of discovering new islands. I recommend looking at videos on how to automate wheat farms to make it less tedious.

Dungeons: There are a few preset types of dungeons, and they're not incredibly rewarding. They're procedural in terms of room order and enemy type, but feel very similar regardless. You'll receive several chests at the end of any type of dungeon but the contents will often only end up either filling your inventory or being left behind.

Development: The developers have been consistently updating the game with content and fixes, and it's significantly different from how it was a year ago. Still, I'd like to see some fixes and additional features. Currently, automation can be quite laggy, so I'd like to see some alternative, less laggy methods of item transportation. Entities will also despawn regardless of whether they're an animal in a farm or (apparently) a robot farming crops, so fixing this should be another priority. However, the developers seem to be focusing on adding more late-game content and fixes, so patience in regards to automation may be important.

Translation: For the most part, everything's understandable. Some translations are missing (item description is too long), and some are just humorous ("This red fruit sometimes contains a human being inside. So please be careful when you want to have a bite. Hermits will be born from small peaches; heroes will be born from large peaches.").

Music: Limited and repetitive, I recommend playing your own music.

Summary: Jack-of-all-Trades, no specialization. There's enough content and entertainment as-is to recommend as long as you're fine with the lack of polish that is typical with Early Access games. This game is really, REALLY fun, BUT, it has 2 major issues. 

I will start this review by briefly stating that the only reason I played this game again is because I already had gotten all of its achievements on Xbox when it was available on game pass in like early 2022, it wasn't that hard to 100% back then, how hard could it be to 100% now? it was freaking HARD, it was not only a completely different game than what I remembered (thanks to seamless mode) but it was way more challenging combat wise this time around.

As for the positives of this game? it's a lovely game to get lost in, there's a HUGE map begging for you to jump in and explore it, pair that with beautiful music and as soon as those first piano notes hit you it already starts to feels like a grand adventure before you even leave the first area/village. During your exploration you'll come across plenty of caves to loot, secrets to be discovered and resources to be gathered that will gradually make you stronger, allowing you to take on even stronger enemies and clear some dungeon puzzles while you're at it. Talking strictly about combat? There's potential for a variety of combat builds to be made, quite a lot of room for experimentation based on the types of weapon and enchantments this game offers, not to mention the amount of skills you can unlock, I am confident you'll find a built that perfectly suits you.

This game has it all; from resource automation, to literal monster petting/collecting. It's extremely easy to sink a bunch of hours on any of its 4 main aspects: Automation, Building, Exploration, & Combat, I only engaged with the later 2 the most, as automation and building are not quite my cup of tea, but the engagement I had with those 2 was phenomenal.

The 2 major issues I briefly mentioned at the beginning are quite literally a deal breaker if you can't get past them, so here they are:

#1: Optimization.

Yup, this game runs BAD, this is the first major issue and it will hit you in the face right away, not even with an upper-mid-range rig like mine's that's specifically tailored for 1440p on modern AAA games, not even then was I able to keep a stable 60fps with a decent render resolution, render distance or shadows activated, as soon as you try to aim for medium settings the game drops to low 40s and to be honest I preferred to just straight up run everything on low to keep it locked to 60fps (Not always, as it still continued to drop by the end game, I accumulated a bunch of resources and needed to pile up chests to store then, lol) THANK GOD I decided to come back in late 2025 because when seamless dropped in mid 2023 this game used to run on low 20s! can you believe that? It did improve, but it's nowhere near where it should be.

But yeah it runs bad and DON'T get me started on the crashes, sometimes I couldn't even play for 5mins straight without having it crash on me, time and time and time and time again, if you play this game make sure to disable auto save and keep saving yourself manually every so often, because the auto save feature defaults to "once ever 30mins" and trust me it will crash by then, and then it'll crash again as soon as you open the game for good measure, losing progress on this game does not feel good at all, and no, this is not something you can control or predict this game has no trigger, it literally just crashes out of nowhere, without even nothing crazy happening on the screen, sometimes you'd be putting points into a new skill you want to try out and then BOOM it crashes, so be on the ready! 

#2: Palworld...? Palworld. 

This is the same developer that launched Palworld way back in 2024 and WOW, wouldn't you figure? they would definitely want to support the top #3 all time steam charts game rather than their failed 2020 attempt, right? RIGHT?

Of course they will rather support their biggest game yet, so yeah, it's literally abandoned as Palworld goes into its 1.0 update, Craftopia continues to receive no real updates for several months, and the only reason it has not been kicked out of early access by Steam at this point it's because Pocketpair drops a patch every once in a while to fix some really dumb a$$ bugs or glitches like "a flower being darker in color than intended", what the hell is even that? so yeah, don't expect any meaningful updates in the future, what you see now is what you get.

So yeah, choose wisely! and oh... get it on S A L E :').

Craftopia is like a teenage relationship. It's fun, it's exciting, you get an overwhelming feeling of anxiety when apart. Yet, it's also immature and prone to missteps ultimately leading to frustration.

As of the time of this review what you're getting with Craftopia is jack of all trades master of none experience. You've got exploration (albeit on limited sized islands). You've got dungeons and rpg elements (albeit simple dungeons and imbalanced skills). You've got base building (albeit with limited options and janky placement). You've got automation (albeit still needing a lot of hand holding and hit or miss success).

I think you get the idea and this runs through nearly all elements of the game, an initial WOW factor and then just under the surface the deficiencies become apparent.So why the positive review? Well of course this is Early Access and you do have a solid foundation here to build a game upon. While the entry price is high for an Early Access title in this state I, personally, weighed up the risk of the game never achieving its goals (and that is entirely possible given the small dev team) with the fact that the only way it can have the possibility to achieve the goals is to be adequately funded.

As such, while I recommend this, I do so warning all potential buyers that you must accept you're taking a big gamble. You'll get some fun out of the game as it stands right now but it's not complete and frankly may never be the game it deserves to be. The choice is yours and in this case you really are making that risky choice to participate in the Early Access development.

It's also probably worth noting that FPS in the game's current state is pretty poor even with a 1080TI in my system I've seen it drop to 15fps at times and rarely get above 40fps. This is made worse once you start building and laying down automation. Those with medium and low spec systems may want to wait until there is a performance pass on the roadmap or take advantage of the refund system to test it out on your system.

I re-installed this game today (06.29.2021) because I wanted to get in a quick play to see if much progress had been made since my last time playing, which was last year.  I couldn't get into the game much before due to all of the issues with it, but saw there were a lot of updates and thought I'd try it again.

Sadly it seems the devs may have reached too far. They set some lofty expectations for this game, mashing together numerous genres and mechanics and as of now it actually seems a bit more janky than when it first came out.  Sure, there were some improvements, but I'd be hard pressed to point out many of them.  It is still Early Access, so hopefully they finish & fix it, but I don't know if they can fix all of the issues with this game because some of it appears due to the actual design choices they made.

[hr]                                                           [/hr]

[h1]++PROS++[/h1]
  +  The crafting isn't bad and there is a ton of stuff to craft with a mostly natural progression
  +  The exploration via different 'islands' (biomes) that you access via portals also isn't bad
  +  You advance through "Ages" that you unlock via items you craft - again, an interesting feature
  +  There are combat skills, magic, and several others so you can somewhat customize your playstyle
  +  They have pets, sort of

Unfortunately, the areas in which the game falls apart are due to some sad choices made by the dev team, so let's check those out.

[h1]--CONS--[/h1]

  - Needs optimization, but it is still Early Access, so that I can at least forgive

  - They give you very small storage chests and even when you can scale up to the larger ones it still isn't enough because of one thing - there are numerous iterations of almost every resource and weapon, but wait it gets worse.  In your personal inventory you'll see that you have 23 fangs that show up in one slot with 4 small fang icons because it combines four different types of those fangs into one slot - when you go to put those into a chest you'll find that you now have 4 slots taken up by those same fangs because they have different stats from one another and storage chests won't combine them.  You'll have X's Fang, Y's Fang, Z's Fang, etc. - I currently have eight different fangs taking up eight slots in one chest - now imagine that for every resource in the game (ore, eggs, feathers, wood, etc.)...

  -  Combat isn't too good either due to the way it is implemented and due to your character automatically facing whichever enemy is the closest once they're right next to you - I've been mining or chopping trees down only to find myself suddenly facing a friendly/enemy mob and hacking at them instead - which is funny because there is no auto-aim.  Then the default dodge key is 'C' while all your combat moves are on the hotkeys - but you can't get all of the skills (melee, magic, harvesting, etc.) on one hotbar, so you'll have to switch between the [i]three[/i] using 'Z' only.

  - The game doesn't pause - you'll hit the [ESC] key to bring up the menu, but if you leave it there your hunger will continue to go down and any nearby enemies may still attack you - seeing as how singleplayer and multiplayer are two different modes you select prior to starting the game, a true pause should be included.

  - The building, ahhhh, the building.  For a game that is supposed to be about crafting & building, they sure messed this up.  Most of the time you can't build how you want because when you try to put down a floor/foundation it doesn't work because it is under the terrain or the terrain isn't flat enough - and no, there aren't any terraforming options either.  So you either start your build in the side of a hill, extend from there, and try to hide the big gaps underneath OR you build your floor hovering above the ground and hide the big gap underneath - I'm quite unsure of what they were going for here, but it looks like some janky Fortnite building ripoff.  Also, every screenshot on this page with a building/farm on it shows flat land - man, if only I could actually find those spots in the game...

[h1]===Final Summation===[/h1]

There IS a lot to like about this game, but between all of the unimplemented features (lots of items & skills currently say WIP), the bugs, janky building & combat, you'd have to be a hardcore fan of the genre to get this right now.  You CAN enjoy it, but it will come with a lot of frustration.  I'm just getting into the automation stuff myself and I'm finding that a lot of things don't work they way you'd expect based on how they are presented - it turns out that a lot of the game is this way.

I currently don't recommend it for the majority of people (you casual folks), but if you want to show some support or you're the patient type, go ahead and dig in.

What happens when you throw elements from several other games into one big pot, give it a stir and some sprinkles, and make a game out of it? Craftopia comes out.

And yet, it... works? And it works incredibly well?

It's almost schizophrenic. You're thrown from laughing your butt off from the hilarious translation ("The goblin screamed, which made everyone drunk"), to an actually engaging bossfight, to a resource gathering process, while exploring a massive map, with SO many different features and builds for character skills... and did I mention it has VRoid integration? You can import your own avatar.

Reminds me of that quote: "A good artist copies. Great Artists steal". It's the game that shouldn't be this good, and yet it is. It's my go-to comfort game at the moment

Automatic stuff is honestly one of the worst things about the game even though it comes off as cool, the bladed machines are terrible to use, crops grow back faster than it can cut down because it stops after hitting something and then slowly rotates, since it can only go in a straight line, the picking up log machine is so pointless since it goes really high into the sky, slowly back down to grab one log, then flies up and slowly down onto the pad and drops the one log.
4. Farming is boring and rather pointless at the moment except for wheat farming or getting to the point to be able to make peaches, since the auto machines are lacking, it basically forces you to either use the exploit of stacking things or manually do all of it.

The way to get batteries which is using the spinning generators (picture in store page) is very annoying to bother with since you have to basically become a pokemon trainer to capture monsters to put them onto the generators (I do believe it gets easier once you use a breeder and keep them all in a pen) but it still doesn't change it being annoying.
6. obviously being early access it is missing a lot of content, so the overall of stuff is lacking so far(armours, need for higher resources etc)

The dungeons are pretty boring and lacking, which they have said to be changing but only by adding in new enemies which doesn't really change much of it and unfortunately the only reason to bother with them is to get tokens to upgrade health, stam and magic (which requires 3 to upgrade one of them slightly but you only get 1 from a dungeon, if you get one at all)

9. the vehicle system is honestly a joke at the moment, hard to control, crash into things constantly or drive it into water (vehicles lose health and explode) and you can't pick them up, so once they are placed, they are stuck in that map, so you can't map jump with the same one.

Though the inventory system is fantastic, it isn't flawless, what drags it down is the annoying way items work, you can have cow hide (they all have their own buffs) a bear hide and a lizard hide which they won't stack into each other, so if you have one of each, they take up 3 different stacks in one slot. (this applies to every material in the game)

This is a game that's like playing a game made by aliens. Everything functions, but none of it functions like you think it should. Crafting, farming, breeding animals- It's all a truly bizarre experience. This makes it entertaining, and it's unique, but it also just has a lot of limitations that makes it less than stellar.

It's only a fun game with friends. You can't play with friends. I know the game says co-op, but once you start trying to play with more than one other person, you'll realize where the problems are. You're basically leashed to each other, forced to stay on the same island in a world that is theoretically massive, meaning that if you're not one hundred percent in line with other people and what they want, you're gonna be arguing about where to go and what to do and what to focus on.

It is a game that tries to do so many things at once but ended up having noting perfect.
I see what Craftopia wants to be -- a sand box universe that gives players freedom for doing various things ranging from adventure to farming. It has its charm even though it is in Early Access and it indeed contains a huge load of bugs.

However, playing single player in this isn't so bad at all. The bugs I found were not so critical that I had to ragequit, no. They are acceptable bugs that are foreseeable because of the tag Early Access per se.
I still do recommend this game for those who are looking for a game to spend some time with in this genre.

Although, multiplayer is not complete at the moment. Too many annoying bugs are around. I don't recommend buying the game just to play muitplayer. Just go solo for now and you are good.

This game exists in a strange place; It looks like an asset flip, feels like an asset flip, sounds like an asset flip, but has the soul of a game that someone cares about. To start with, the game looks and sounds awful. There's no consistency with the art, anime humans are next to realistic animals are next to chibi slimes are next to dark souls weapons. You ride a hoverboard through an Aztec ruin while dressed like a medieval European peasant. All the sound effects are grating, notably the seagulls sound like a squeaky toy for some reason. None of the crafting stations look like they should be next to each other.

The "Enchantment" system is actually pretty novel, but lacks polish. In short, getting resources from certain sources holds certain modifiers, so leather from a bear grants a different bonus than leather from a deer. In practice, this causes your inventory to be filled with garbage that won't stack. While inside your inventory you can stack 4 like materials, in a chest they don't, meaning that two inventory spaces can turn to 8 spaces in a chest. This wouldn't be awful except for the fact that (At least the first three) storage options suck, only giving 8,16, and 24 spaces, with the 16 space one being a gigantic piece of machinery. 

I think this game has a lot of good ideas, but badly needs to organize itself and make considerable quality of life changes.
